name: Ahasuerus
title: King of Persia and husband of Esther
summary: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian great king Xerxes I, who ruled over the Achaemenid world empire with its 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. In the book of Esther, he appears as a powerful but easily influenced ruler who allows himself to be guided by his advisors—first when he deposes Queen Vashti after her disobedience, and then when the nobleman Haman is given authority to issue a decree for the destruction of all Jews in the empire. It is through Queen Esther's life-risking approach to the king that God's hidden providence becomes evident: the Jewish people are saved from ruin, Haman is executed on his own gallows, and Mordecai is elevated to the second most powerful position in the empire. Remarkably, God's name is never mentioned directly in the book of Esther, yet the entire story testifies to His sovereign rule behind the scenes of history. These events laid the foundation for the festival of Purim, which is still celebrated in Jewish tradition as a commemoration of God's liberating intervention. Ahasuerus is also mentioned in Ezra 4:6, where opponents of the rebuilding in Jerusalem sent written accusations against him early in his reign, shedding further light on his role in the history of the Jewish diaspora.

keyEvents.title: The Great Banquet
keyEvents.description: Ahasuerus held a magnificent banquet for all his princes and servants that lasted 180 days, to display the wealth and glory of his kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Queen Vashti Deposed
keyEvents.description: When Queen Vashti refused to obey the king's command to appear before his guests, she was deposed as queen on the advice of his counselors.

keyEvents.title: Esther Chosen as Queen
keyEvents.description: After an extensive search for a new queen, Esther, a Jewish woman and Mordecai's adopted daughter, was chosen because she won the king's favor above all other women.

keyEvents.title: Mordecai Exposes the Conspiracy
keyEvents.description: Mordecai discovered a conspiracy by two of the king's officials, Bigthan and Teresh, who planned to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. Mordecai told Esther, who reported it to the king. The matter was investigated and confirmed, and the two were executed. The event was recorded in the king's chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Ahasuerus gave Haman authority to issue a decree to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom, after Haman was offended that Mordecai refused to bow down before him.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Courageous Approach to the King
keyEvents.description: Esther risked her life by going uninvited into the king's presence, but Ahasuerus extended his golden scepter toward her and showed her favor. She invited the king and Haman to a banquet, where she revealed Haman's evil plan against her people.

keyEvents.title: The King's Sleepless Night
keyEvents.description: Ahasuerus could not sleep and had the chronicles read to him, discovering that Mordecai had never been rewarded for exposing the conspiracy against the king. This became a turning point in the story.

keyEvents.title: The Jews Are Saved and Haman Is Executed
keyEvents.description: When Ahasuerus heard about Haman's plot, he was furious and ordered that Haman be hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. The king issued a new decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves, and Mordecai was elevated to a prominent position in the kingdom.

versions.summary: Ahasuerus, also known as Xerxes I, was the Persian king who ruled over a vast empire from India to Ethiopia. He is best known from the Book of Esther, where he chose the Jewish woman Esther as his queen, and through her influence, the Jewish people were saved from destruction planned by Haman. His reign marked an important period for the Jewish diaspora in the Persian Empire.

footnotes.text: Ahasuerus is identified by most historians with Xerxes I of Persia (reign c. 486–465 BC), son of Darius I and Atossa. The Hebrew name "Ahasuerus" (אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, Aḥashverosh) is a Hebrew rendering of the Old Persian name Xšayāršā, which became Xerxes in Greek.

Archaeological excavations at Susa (the biblical Shushan) have uncovered remains of the Persian palace (apadana) that match descriptions in the Book of Esther, including the richly decorated columned hall and the inner garden mentioned in Est 1:5–6. Inscriptions from Xerxes I have also been found at the site, confirming his close connection to this palace.

The Purim festival, celebrated by Jews on the 14th and 15th of Adar (February/March), originates from the events described in the Book of Esther during Ahasuerus' reign. The name "Purim" comes from the Akkadian word "pūru", meaning lot, because Haman cast lots to choose the date for the destruction of the Jews (Est 3:7; 9:24–26).

The Greek historian Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC) gives a detailed account of Xerxes I, including his massive military campaign against Greece in 480 BC (the battles of Thermopylae and Salamis). These events likely took place between the deposition of Vashti and Esther's selection as queen, which may explain the several-year gap between the events in Est 1 and Est 2.

In Jewish tradition (Talmud, Megilla 11a–13a), Ahasuerus' character is discussed extensively. Some rabbis view him as a foolish ruler who was easily manipulated, while others see him as a calculating politician. The Midrash tradition also expands on the background of Vashti's rejection and Esther's role at court.

Ahasuerus is mentioned in Ezra 4:6, where it is reported that opponents of Judah and Benjamin sent accusations against the inhabitants of Jerusalem at the beginning of his reign. This shows that the Persian king was involved in political matters affecting the Jewish people even outside the narrative of the Book of Esther.

Xerxes I's mother Atossa was the daughter of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Achaemenid Empire. This family connection gave Xerxes strong dynastic legitimacy. Atossa is described by Herodotus as a very influential woman at the Persian court, and she is said to have played a key role in Xerxes being chosen as heir over his older brothers.

The Book of Esther is unique among biblical writings because God's name is never explicitly mentioned. Nevertheless, Jewish and Christian interpreters throughout history have seen God's providence working behind the scenes in the story's events—from Esther's elevation to queen to the decisive night when the king could not sleep and had the chronicle of Mordecai's service read aloud (Est 6:1–3).
